chapters.name: Chapter 1: Cloud concepts and Azure's building blocks

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What the cloud is and why organizations use it
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain cloud computing and its main benefits with an everyday example.
This lesson builds toward: Given an everyday example such as a busy food bank website, you will explain what cloud computing is and name its main benefits and cloud models, in your own words, with at least two correct benefits.
Cloud computing means renting computing power, storage and software over the internet instead of buying and running your own servers. Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud are the biggest cloud providers.
It is like electricity: you do not build a power plant, you plug in and pay for what you use. This is called the consumption-based or pay-as-you-go model. Instead of a big upfront purchase (capital expense, CapEx), you pay a running cost (operating expense, OpEx).
Main benefits: scalability (add more power when a food bank's sign-up page gets busy, then shrink it), high availability (it keeps running if one machine fails), reliability, security tools, and easier management. There are three cloud models: public (shared provider like Azure), private (used by one organization only) and hybrid (a mix of both).
Words to know:
- Cloud computing: renting computing power, storage and software over the internet.
- Consumption-based model: you pay only for what you use.
- CapEx / OpEx: capital expense is a big upfront purchase; operating expense is an ongoing cost.
- Scalability: adding or removing resources as demand changes.
- High availability: a service keeps running even when parts fail.
- Hybrid cloud: a mix of public cloud and an organization's own private systems.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900
Try it now: Pick a local organization you know (a church, clinic, school, food bank or small shop). Write two ways it could use the cloud and which benefit (scalability, availability, pay-as-you-go) each one gives it.
You can now explain cloud computing, the pay-as-you-go model, its benefits and the three cloud models.

check.q: What is OpEx in cloud computing?
options: A big upfront purchase of servers
A running cost you pay as you use the service
A free trial that never ends
check.why: Pay-as-you-go turns a big upfront purchase (CapEx) into a running operating expense (OpEx).

check.q: A clinic must keep some data on its own servers but wants Azure for its website. Which cloud model fits?
check.why: Hybrid cloud mixes an organization's own servers with a public cloud like Azure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and who is responsible for what
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort a service into IaaS, PaaS or SaaS and say who handles what.
This lesson builds toward: Given a cloud service, you will sort it into IaaS, PaaS or SaaS and say what the provider and the customer each protect, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Cloud services come in three types. IaaS (infrastructure as a service): you rent virtual machines and networks and manage almost everything on them yourself, like renting an empty apartment. PaaS (platform as a service): the provider runs the servers and system software; you bring your app or data, like a furnished apartment. SaaS (software as a service): you just use finished software, like Outlook email or Microsoft Teams, like a hotel room.
Serverless is a kind of PaaS where your code runs only when something triggers it and you pay per use, with no server to manage at all (Azure Functions is an example).
The shared responsibility model says who protects what. The provider always secures the physical datacenters. You are always responsible for your data, your accounts and who has access. In between, the more you move from IaaS to SaaS, the more the provider handles.
Step by step:
- Ask: do we manage the operating system? If yes, it is IaaS.
- Do we only bring our app or data? Then it is PaaS.
- Do we just log in and use the software? Then it is SaaS.
- Remember: your data and accounts are always your job.
Words to know:
- IaaS: infrastructure as a service: you rent virtual machines and manage them.
- PaaS: platform as a service: the provider runs the platform; you bring your app.
- SaaS: software as a service: ready-to-use software over the internet.
- Serverless: code that runs only when triggered, with no server for you to manage.
- Shared responsibility model: how security jobs are split between the cloud provider and you.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900
Try it now: Sort these into IaaS, PaaS or SaaS: Microsoft Outlook email, an Azure virtual machine, Azure App Service for a website, Microsoft Teams, Azure Functions. Then write one thing you are always responsible for, no matter which type.
You can now tell IaaS, PaaS and SaaS apart and explain the shared responsibility model.

check.q: Which type is like renting a furnished apartment: the provider runs the servers and you bring your app?
check.why: In PaaS the provider runs servers and system software; you bring your app or data.

check.q: Your nonprofit moves from IaaS to SaaS. What happens to its security work?
options: It must now guard the datacenter
The provider handles more, but your data and accounts are still your job
The provider becomes responsible for your passwords
check.why: Moving toward SaaS shifts more work to the provider, but your data and access always stay yours.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: How Azure is organized: regions, zones and resource groups
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Describe where Azure runs and how resources are organized and found in the Azure portal.
This lesson builds toward: For a small Azure project, you will choose a region and a resource group and describe how they fit into a subscription, with a reason for the region you choose.
Azure runs in datacenters around the world grouped into regions, such as East US or South Africa North. You choose a region for each thing you build: closer to your users is usually faster, and some data has rules about which country it must stay in. Many regions have availability zones: separate datacenters with their own power and cooling, so if one fails, another keeps running. Regions are also paired with another region in the same geography for disaster recovery.
Everything you create (a virtual machine, a database, a storage account) is a resource. Resources go into resource groups, folders for things that belong together, like everything for one website. Resource groups sit in a subscription, which is the billing account. Large organizations group subscriptions with management groups.
You manage all of it in the Azure portal, a website at portal.azure.com. You can also use Azure Cloud Shell, the Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell to manage it by typing commands.
Step by step:
- Choose a region close to your users that meets any data rules.
- Use availability zones when the service must stay up.
- Put related resources in one resource group.
- Know which subscription pays for them.
- Manage it all in the Azure portal or with command-line tools.
Words to know:
- Region: a geographic area with one or more Azure datacenters.
- Availability zone: a separate datacenter in a region with its own power, cooling and network.
- Resource: anything you create in Azure, like a virtual machine or database.
- Resource group: a folder that holds related resources.
- Subscription: the account that Azure charges are billed to.
- Management group: a way to group several subscriptions under shared rules.
- Azure portal: the website for managing Azure.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900
Try it now: Plan the structure for a community center that wants a website and a place to store sign-up forms: name a resource group, list two resources that go in it, and pick a region near you. Write one reason for your region choice.
You can now explain regions, availability zones, resources, resource groups, subscriptions and management groups.

check.q: What is a resource group in Azure?
options: A folder for resources that belong together, like one website
check.why: Resource groups hold related resources; the subscription is the billing account.

check.q: Your users are in South Africa and their data must stay in the country. How do you pick a region?
options: Pick a region close to your users that meets the data rules
check.why: Choose a region close to users that also meets any rules about where data must stay.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Core services, cost and your certification

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Core Azure services: compute, networking, storage and databases
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Match a common need to the right core Azure service.
This lesson builds toward: Given a common need such as a website, a full server or backups, you will match the need to the right core Azure service, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Compute runs your programs. Azure Virtual Machines give you a full computer in the cloud (IaaS). Azure App Service hosts websites and web apps without managing servers (PaaS). Containers package an app with everything it needs so it runs the same anywhere. Azure Functions runs small pieces of code when triggered (serverless). Azure Virtual Desktop gives people a Windows desktop they can reach from any device.
Networking connects things. An Azure virtual network is your private network in the cloud. A VPN Gateway links it to your office over the internet; ExpressRoute is a private connection that does not go over the public internet. Azure DNS turns names into addresses.
Storage keeps files and data. A storage account holds Blob storage (photos, videos, backups), Azure Files (shared folders), queues and tables. Storage tiers (hot, cool, cold, archive) cost less the less often you open the files. Redundancy options keep extra copies so a failure does not lose data. For databases, Azure has managed options such as Azure SQL Database and Azure Cosmos DB.
Step by step:
- Need a website? Look at Azure App Service.
- Need full control of a server? Azure Virtual Machines.
- Need code to run on an event? Azure Functions.
- Need to store files or backups? A storage account with Blob storage.
- Rarely opened files? Use a cooler, cheaper tier.
Words to know:
- Virtual machine (VM): a computer that runs as software in the cloud.
- Azure App Service: a PaaS service for hosting websites and web apps.
- Container: a package of an app and everything it needs to run.
- Virtual network: a private network for your Azure resources.
- Blob storage: storage for large files like photos, videos and backups.
- Storage tier: a price level based on how often you open the data: hot, cool, cold or archive.
- Redundancy: keeping extra copies so data survives a failure.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900
Try it now: For the community center from Lesson 3, choose a service for each need: a public website, a place to keep scanned sign-up forms, and old photos that are almost never opened. Write which service and, for the photos, which storage tier.
You can now match common needs to Azure compute, networking, storage and database services.

check.q: Which Azure service runs small pieces of code only when something triggers it?
check.why: Azure Functions is serverless: code runs when triggered, and you pay per use.

check.q: A youth center needs a shared folder its staff can all open. What would you suggest?
options: Azure Files in a storage account
check.why: Azure Files in a storage account provides shared folders.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Security, governance and controlling costs
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Name the Azure tools that keep accounts safe, enforce rules and stop surprise bills.
This lesson builds toward: For the people and resources in your plan, you will list how you will protect sign-in and access and enforce rules with MFA, RBAC, tags, Azure Policy or resource locks, naming at least three of these tools and what each does. Using the free Azure pricing calculator and Microsoft Learn, you will estimate a monthly cost for your plan and write an AZ-900 study plan, with an estimated total and your two weakest exam areas.
Identity: Microsoft Entra ID is Azure's sign-in and directory service. Turn on multifactor authentication (MFA), which asks for a second proof such as a code in an app, so a stolen password is not enough. Single sign-on (SSO) lets people use one account for many apps. Role-based access control (RBAC) gives each person only the access their job needs. Zero Trust means never assume a request is safe; always verify.
Governance: Azure Policy sets rules, such as "only create resources in these regions". Resource locks stop important resources from being deleted or changed by accident. Tags are labels like department=youth or project=website that help you sort and track costs. Microsoft Defender for Cloud checks your setup for security problems.
Costs: what you pay depends on the service, its size, the region, how long it runs and how much data leaves Azure. The free Azure pricing calculator estimates a monthly cost before you build anything. Cost Management lets you set budgets and alerts. A simple rule: delete what you do not use.
Step by step:
- Turn on MFA for every account.
- Give people only the access their job needs (RBAC).
- Add tags to every resource.
- Use Azure Policy and resource locks for important rules.
- Estimate costs first in the pricing calculator, then set a budget alert.
Words to know:
- Microsoft Entra ID: Microsoft's cloud sign-in and directory service.
- Multifactor authentication (MFA): signing in with a password plus a second proof.
- RBAC: role-based access control: access based on a person's job.
- Zero Trust: a security approach: never assume trust, always verify.
- Azure Policy: a tool that enforces rules on what can be created.
- Resource lock: stops a resource being deleted or changed by mistake.
- Tag: a label on a resource used to sort it and track costs.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900
- Microsoft Azure: Pricing calculator
Try it now: Write three safety and cost rules for the community center's Azure setup, one each for sign-in, access and spending. Example: "Every volunteer account uses MFA." Then write two tags you would put on every resource.
You can now describe how Azure keeps accounts safe, enforces rules and keeps costs under control.

options: Trust every request from inside the office
Always verify; never assume a request is safe
check.why: Zero Trust means every request is checked instead of assumed safe.

check.q: A volunteer's password was stolen, but the thief could not sign in. Which setting most likely stopped them?
check.why: MFA asks for a second proof, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Estimating costs and planning your AZ-900 path
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Estimate a monthly cost in the pricing calculator and make a study plan for AZ-900.
This lesson builds toward: Using the free Azure pricing calculator and Microsoft Learn, you will estimate a monthly cost for your plan and write an AZ-900 study plan, with an estimated total and your two weakest exam areas.
The pricing calculator is free on Microsoft's website. You add the services you plan to use, choose a region and options like size and hours, and it shows an estimated monthly cost. Prices change and depend on region, so always use the calculator instead of a number you read somewhere.
If you want to practice in Azure itself, Microsoft offers a free account with some services free for 12 months and over 65 services free every month up to set amounts, for new customers. Read the current terms on Microsoft's free services page before you sign up, set a budget alert, and delete practice resources when you finish. Students may qualify for a separate Azure for Students offer with an academic email.
The exam for the Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals certification is AZ-900. Microsoft's study guide lists three areas: cloud concepts (25-30%), Azure architecture and services (35-40%), and Azure management and governance (30-35%). You need a score of 700 or more to pass. The exam page lists 45 minutes for the assessment, and the price depends on the country where you take it, so check it there. Microsoft Learn has free training and a free practice assessment.
Step by step:
- Open the Azure pricing calculator.
- Add the services from your plan, choose your region and sizes.
- Write down the estimated monthly total.
- Open the AZ-900 page on Microsoft Learn and take the free practice assessment.
- List your two weakest areas and the free Microsoft Learn modules for them.
Words to know:
- Pricing calculator: Microsoft's free tool to estimate Azure costs before you build.
- AZ-900: the exam code for Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals.
- Practice assessment: free practice questions on Microsoft Learn that show your readiness.
- Microsoft Learn: Microsoft's free training and certification website.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Azure: Pricing calculator
- Microsoft Azure: Free services
- Microsoft Learn: Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals
- Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900
Try it now: Final task: write the one-page Azure plan for a community organization's website and file storage (services and type, region, resource group, safe sign-in, tags and budget), add the monthly estimate from the pricing calculator, then take the free AZ-900 practice assessment and list your two weakest areas.
You can now plan and price a small Azure setup and follow a clear path to the AZ-900 certification.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Service type and services The plan names no Azure services, or they do not fit a website and file storage. Names the service type (IaaS, PaaS or SaaS) and fitting services, such as App Service and a storage account. Says why each service fits better than another choice. Region and organization No region or resource group is named. Names a region with a reason and puts the resources in one resource group. Also names the subscription that pays and whether availability zones are needed. Safe sign-in and rules Does not say how people sign in or who can do what. Uses MFA and gives each person only the access they need (RBAC). Also adds tags, a policy or a resource lock and says what each protects. Cost estimate No estimate, or a number not taken from the pricing calculator. Gives an estimated monthly total from the pricing calculator and a budget alert. Names one change that would lower the cost, such as a cooler storage tier. Study plan The practice assessment was not taken. Took the free practice assessment and listed the two weakest areas. Linked each weak area to a free Microsoft Learn module and a date to study it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why use the Azure pricing calculator instead of a price you read online?
options: Prices change and depend on region, so the calculator gives a current estimate
The calculator signs you up automatically
check.why: Prices change and differ by region, so estimate with the calculator for your own choices.

check.q: You took the free AZ-900 practice assessment. What is the best next step?
options: Book the exam today without studying
Retake it until you memorize the answers
List your two weakest areas and find the free Microsoft Learn modules for them
Stop, because practice scores do not matter
check.why: Your weakest areas show where to study next, and Microsoft Learn has free modules for each.
